common_name: Biker Billy Jalapeño Pepper (AAS-Winning Long Mild Jalapeño)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Biker Billy is an All-America Selections winning jalapeño bred for unusually long, slender fruit and earlier, more prolific production than standard jalapeños, with milder, more consistent heat.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Biker Billy, named for a television chili-pepper personality, was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for producing notably long, slender jalapeño fruits, up to 5-6 inches, considerably longer than standard jalapeño varieties, along with earlier maturity and heavier overall yield. Heat is milder and more consistent than many jalapeño varieties, which can vary widely in spiciness depending on growing conditions, making Biker Billy a more predictable choice for recipes needing reliable, moderate jalapeño heat. Fruits ripen from dark green to red and can be harvested at either stage, with red fruit slightly sweeter. Its high productivity and vigorous, disease-resistant plants make it a dependable choice for home gardens and market growers alike. Harvest regularly to encourage continued fruit set through the season.

common_name: Trinidad Perfume Pepper (Heatless Aromatic Habanero-Type Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Trinidad Perfume is a heatless habanero-type pepper prized for the intense fruity, floral, apricot-like aroma and flavor typical of Capsicum chinense peppers, without any of the heat.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Trinidad Perfume is a heatless selection within the Capsicum chinense species, the same species as habaneros and Scotch bonnets, bred to capture the intensely fruity, floral, almost apricot-and-citrus aroma and flavor characteristic of that species without any of the fiery heat, making it usable in far larger quantities than a true habanero for salsas, sauces, and dishes where habanero flavor is wanted but the heat is not. The wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits look nearly identical to a habanero, ripening from green to orange or red, and can be used fresh, dried, or blended into sauces for a burst of tropical fruit flavor. Plants are productive and grow similarly to other Capsicum chinense peppers, benefiting from a long, warm growing season. Harvest regularly to encourage continued fruit set through the season.

common_name: Butch T Trinidad Scorpion Pepper (Former World's Hottest Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Butch T Trinidad Scorpion once held the Guinness World Record for the hottest pepper in the world, with extreme heat well over one million Scoville Heat Units, requiring careful handling with gloves.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Butch T Trinidad Scorpion, a selection developed by grower Butch Taylor, held the Guinness World Record for the world's hottest pepper in 2011, testing over 1.4 million Scoville Heat Units, among the most extreme heat levels achievable in a pepper. The small, wrinkled, scorpion-tail-shaped fruits ripen from green to a deep red and carry the fruity, slightly sweet undertone typical of superhot Capsicum chinense peppers beneath the overwhelming heat. Always wear gloves when handling fresh or dried fruit and avoid touching the face, since the capsaicin can cause serious skin and eye irritation; use in tiny quantities, typically a single pepper diluted into a large batch of hot sauce or infused oil. Plants are moderately productive and benefit from a long, warm growing season and consistent moisture. This is a specialty pepper for heat enthusiasts and hot sauce makers, not general culinary use.

common_name: Carolina Cayenne Pepper (AAS-Winning Early Compact Cayenne)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Carolina Cayenne is an All-America Selections winning cayenne bred for earlier maturity and a more compact, uniform plant than traditional cayenne varieties, with classic thin, curved, hot red fruit.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Carolina Cayenne was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining classic cayenne heat and flavor with notably earlier maturity and a more compact, well-branched plant habit than older cayenne varieties, making it a reliable choice for gardeners with a shorter growing season or limited space. Fruits are thin, curved, and about 5-6 inches long, ripening from green to bright red with the sharp, straightforward heat cayenne is known for, well suited to drying, grinding into cayenne powder, or using fresh in cooking. The compact plants are heavily productive relative to their size, and the early maturity allows for a longer overall harvest window within the growing season. Harvest regularly, or let a portion of the crop ripen fully red and dry on or off the plant for storage as dried cayenne.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Cheyenne is a classic All-America Selections winning cayenne cultivar bred for a compact, upright habit with fruit held above the foliage, making harvest easy and keeping pods off the ground.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Cheyenne is a long-established All-America Selections winning cayenne cultivar bred for a compact, upright plant that holds its thin, curved, hot red pods well above the foliage rather than letting them dangle near the soil, keeping fruit cleaner and easier to spot and harvest. The classic sharp cayenne heat and flavor make it well suited to drying and grinding into cayenne powder, pickling, or fresh use in cooking. Its compact size makes it a good choice for containers and smaller garden beds where a sprawling pepper plant would be impractical. Harvest regularly for fresh use, or let a portion of the crop ripen fully red and dry on the plant for storage as dried cayenne.
